name: Jamal Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays, I'm a site carpenter and crew lead for Ridgeway Homes, a big housebuilder. We're on an estate of two hundred houses on the edge of town, Meadow Rise, and my crew does the roofs, the first fix and the stairs. It's the same five house types over and over, so it's about speed and getting it right first time. Weekends, I run my own little business doing garden rooms and loft conversions, and that's where I really get to think.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you run the weekend business alongside the day job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: AI, mostly. I take photos and a laser scan of someone's loft on a Saturday, and by Sunday night the AI has helped me draft the plan, the materials list and the quote. Stuff that used to take me three evenings takes one. My wife Leila says I talk to the chatbot more than I talk to her, which is unfair, but only a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm keeping it anyway, it's useful. People who thought it was magic will be disappointed, people who thought it was the end of the world will be relieved, and I'll still be using it for my quotes. I'd say that at the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. It saves me time on the weekend business and that's all I needed from it. Ridgeway wouldn't change much, the houses would keep going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep both jobs going. I'd keep using AI for the quotes and maybe take on one more loft a month, since the paperwork's quicker. I'd keep paying the mortgage down and saving for Yusuf's braces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little let down, I like new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the weekend business bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four hundred a month after materials, more in summer. It's what pays for the holidays and fills the savings pot. We've got about four months saved and most of that came from lofts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your weekday crew uses AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Kev thinks it's spying on him. I showed him how to use it to check a roof pitch and he looked at me like I'd sold my soul. But he's the best roofer I've ever worked with.

S0.say: I'm keeping it anyway because it's useful: believers will be disappointed, worriers relieved, and I'll still use it for quotes. I'd say that at the canteen.
S0.think: I'd be fine, because it saves time on my weekend business and that's all I needed from it. The houses at Ridgeway would keep going up as before.
S0.do: Keeps both the day job and the weekend business going and takes on one more loft a month thanks to faster paperwork. Keeps paying the mortgage down and saving for his son's braces.
S0.feel: Calm, a little let down because he likes new things.
S0.quote: Kev thinks it's spying on him.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal already runs a side business powered by AI, which gives him a sense of control. His savings mostly come from that weekend work. He is noticeably alone on his crew in using AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's money in this for anyone who gets in early. I'd say it to the lads, and I'd probably post a video of my scanner doing a loft, just to show it's not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the volume sites are the first to change. Five house types, built over and over, that's exactly what machines are good at. So my weekday job might shrink, but my weekend job could grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a better laser scanner and maybe a small cutting machine, a CNC, which is a computer-controlled router, to cut stair parts in my garage. That's two or three thousand out of savings, and I'd want it back within a year. I'd start telling Ridgeway I'd like to be the one who trials any new kit on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two or three thousand is a big chunk of four months' savings. What does Leila say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, show me the numbers. So I'd show her: six lofts with the machine pays it off. She'd say fine, but if it's not paid off by next Christmas, it gets sold. That's fair, that's how we work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd want your weekday job to shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not want, no. But I'd rather see it coming and have the weekend business ready. If Ridgeway brings in robots for roof trusses, I want to be the guy they ask to run them, not the guy they let go.

S1.say: There's money in this for anyone who gets in early. I'd tell the lads and post a video of my scanner doing a loft, just to show it's not scary.
S1.think: Volume sites change first, because five house types built over and over is exactly what machines are good at. My weekday job might shrink while my weekend job grows.
S1.do: Spends two to three thousand of savings on a better laser scanner and a small CNC cutting machine for stair parts, aiming to pay it back within a year. Volunteers at Ridgeway to trial any new kit on site.
S1.quote: If Ridgeway brings in robots for roof trusses, I want to be the guy they ask to run them, not the guy they let go.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal sees exactly why his weekday work is exposed, and responds by investing rather than worrying. He and his wife have a clear rule for risky purchases. His pragmatism is about positioning, not ideology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, this is big, and anyone who isn't paying attention needs to start. I wouldn't say it's a disaster in public, I'd say it's a change. But I'd say it a lot less cheerfully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, two years is too fast even for me. If robots can do the roofs at Ridgeway, they can do lofts too, and my clever weekend business is just a smaller version of the same job. I'd be scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Ridgeway in the first month and ask to be trained to set up and run the robots, whatever they buy. At home I'd stop spending on tools and build up the savings, maybe sell the CNC if I'd bought it. I'd use the weekend business while it lasts to make as much as I can, every Saturday and Sunday. And I'd start asking what jobs need someone who understands both building and machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got moves to make, but I'm not sure they're enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your crew, Kev for example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kev straight: learn this, or you're out, and I'm sorry. He'd tell me to get lost. I'd still put his name down for any course going, because he's got two kids too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your business is a smaller version of the same job. Is there anything a robot couldn't do there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sitting at someone's kitchen table and working out what they actually want. People say loft, but they mean a room where their teenager can't hear them argue. Maybe that part stays human, I honestly don't know.

S2.say: This is big and anyone not paying attention needs to start. I'd call it a change, not a disaster, but I'd say it a lot less cheerfully.
S2.think: Two years is too fast even for me: if robots can do Ridgeway's roofs, they can do lofts too. My weekend business is just a smaller version of the same job.
S2.do: Asks Ridgeway in the first month to train him to set up and run its robots. Stops tool spending, builds savings, possibly sells the CNC, and works every weekend while the side business lasts.
S2.feel: Anxious, with moves to make but doubts they'll be enough.
S2.quote: People say loft, but they mean a room where their teenager can't hear them argue.
S2.fieldNote: Even with his head start, two years leaves him scrambling, because he sees his side business as exposed too. He would push his reluctant colleague onto courses anyway. His hunch that the human part is understanding what clients really want was the most thoughtful line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start for anyone who uses it. I'd be the annoying one at work telling everyone to learn the new tools now. I'd probably post a few how-to videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with five years I think I come out ahead. I'd have time to turn the weekend business into something that uses robots instead of competing with them. The tricky bit is guessing which part of the job stays human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year learning how the building robots work, online courses and whatever Ridgeway trials. By year two or three, I'd want my own business to be the one bringing in a small robot for cutting and fixing, with me doing design and the client side. I'd keep a solid six months of savings and invest the rest into kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before a big job you know you can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Ridgeway in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, around year three. Once the weekend business is steady, I'd go full time on it. Leila's job is steady, so we'd have one sure wage while I take the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Yusuf and Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf likes coding already. I'd push him to keep going and learn to build things too, because the people who can do both will be fine. Nadia's nine, she just wants a horse.

S3.say: Five years is a head start for anyone who uses it. I'd be the annoying one at work telling everyone to learn the new tools now, and I'd post some how-to videos.
S3.think: With five years I think I come out ahead, turning the weekend business into one that uses robots instead of competing with them. The tricky bit is guessing which part of the job stays human.
S3.do: Spends the first year learning building robotics through online courses and Ridgeway trials, and by year two or three brings a small robot into his own business. Keeps six months of savings and invests the rest in kit, likely leaving Ridgeway around year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, like before a big job he knows he can do.
S3.quote: Leila's job is steady, so we'd have one sure wage while I take the risk.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him go on the offence, building a business around the machines. His plan relies on his wife's steady income as a safety net. He thinks the hard part is guessing which piece of the job stays human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, so start now and don't panic. I'd say it to anyone who asked and probably to some who didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is a gift. I'd have my own firm, small, a few machines and a couple of people, doing design and the client side. I'd be fifty-three and running something I built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the weekend business steadily, bring in machines as they get cheaper, and leave Ridgeway when it made sense, maybe year four or five. I'd keep savings healthy, pay the mortgage down, and put money into the business each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pretty hopeful about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where it goes wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone gets the same machines and prices drop to nothing, then my little firm doesn't make money. That's possible, I'll admit it. I'd still rather have a go than sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Kev in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, Kev could make it to an early pension, he's older than me. I'd tell him to hang on and keep his head down. Not everyone needs to change, some people just need to get to the finish line.

S4.say: Ten years is loads of time, so start now and don't panic. I'd say it to anyone who asked, and probably to some who didn't.
S4.think: Ten years is a gift: I'd have my own small firm with a few machines and a couple of people, doing design and the client side. I'd be fifty-three and running something I built.
S4.do: Grows the weekend business steadily and brings in machines as they get cheaper. Leaves Ridgeway around year four or five while keeping savings healthy, paying down the mortgage and investing in the business each year.
S4.quote: Not everyone needs to change, some people just need to get to the finish line.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Jamal sees the change as a path to owning his own firm. He admits a real risk, falling prices when everyone has the same machines. He is generous about colleagues who don't want to change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Even with my head start, there's no time to build anything. What would help is cheap loans for small builders to buy the machines themselves, so it's not just the big firms that own them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people actually want built. Everyone talks about who does the work, but someone still has to sit with the family and work out what they need. That's the part I'd fight to keep.

headlineQuote: Someone still has to sit with the family and work out what they need.
portrait: Jamal Costa is a 43-year-old crew leader on a large new-build housing estate who also runs a weekend business doing lofts and garden rooms, married to a dental hygienist, with two children and about four months saved. He uses AI every day to draft plans and quotes, and his savings largely come from that side work. He's calm under a plateau and steady change, investing in kit and positioning himself to run new machines. Two years leaves him anxious and scrambling, but with five or ten years he'd build his own small firm around robots, keeping the client conversations for himself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because even with his head start there would be no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small builders to buy the machines themselves, so big firms aren't the only owners.
